es.summary: Náuseas que aparecen antes de iniciar un tratamiento, típicamente quimioterapia, como respuesta aprendida al estímulo asociado al procedimiento.
key_points: Se desencadenan por asociación condicionada entre el entorno del tratamiento y la experiencia previa de vómitos.
Factores de riesgo incluyen ansiedad, experiencias previas de náuseas, sexo femenino y edad <50 años.
El manejo primario es no farmacológico: técnicas de relajación, terapia cognitivo‑conductual y desensibilización sistemática.
Los antieméticos pueden usarse como medida preventiva, pero son menos eficaces que las intervenciones conductuales.
Complicaciones potenciales: deshidratación, desequilibrio electrolítico y disminución de la adherencia al tratamiento.

pathophysiology: El estímulo del entorno (sala de quimioterapia, olores) se asocia al CTZ mediante aprendizaje clásico.
El cerebro anticipa la náusea y activa la zona gatadora del quimiorreceptor, liberando dopamina y serotonina.
Se produce una respuesta fisiológica de náusea antes de la exposición al agente quimioterápico.
risk_factors: Experiencias previas de náuseas o vómitos durante tratamientos.
Sexo femenino y edad menor a 50 años.
Sensibilidad a olores o estímulos visuales del entorno de tratamiento.
signs_symptoms: Queja subjetiva de náusea antes de iniciar la terapia.
Aumento de la frecuencia respiratoria y sensación de malestar abdominal.
diagnostics: Historia clínica enfocada en episodios previos y factores desencadenantes.
Evaluación de signos vitales y estado de hidratación.
Exámenes de laboratorio solo si se sospecha deshidratación: Na+, K+ en mEq/L, glucosa en mg/dL.
treatment: Técnicas de relajación profunda y respiración diafragmática antes del tratamiento.
Antieméticos de primera línea como fenotiazinas (p. ej., proclorperazina) o antagonistas 5‑HT3 (ondansetrón) como medida preventiva.
Control del ambiente: reducir olores fuertes, iluminación tenue y ruido mínimo.
complications: Deshidratación y déficit de volumen de líquidos.
Interrupción o retraso del esquema de quimioterapia.
nursing_care: Evaluar nivel de náusea usando escala de 0‑10 antes y después del tratamiento.
Monitorear ingesta y salida; registrar I/O cada 8 h.
Proveer ambiente tranquilo, minimizar estímulos desencadenantes.
Administrar antiemético según prescripción 30‑60 min antes del procedimiento.
Documentar respuesta a intervenciones no farmacológicas.
patient_teaching: Enseñar técnicas de respiración y relajación para usar antes de la sesión.
Informar sobre la importancia de tomar el antiemético preventivo según indicación.
Identificar y evitar estímulos que desencadenen la náusea (olor, alimentos).
Fomentar hidratación adecuada y consumo de alimentos ligeros antes del tratamiento.

evidenced_by: queja de náusea antes de la quimioterapia
outcomes: Náuseas controladas: paciente reporta ≤2 episodios por día

interventions.rationale: Permite cuantificar la intensidad y monitorizar la respuesta

interventions.action: Aplicar técnicas de respiración diafragmática y relajación guiada 10 min antes del procedimiento
interventions.rationale: Reduce la respuesta de ansiedad que desencadena la náusea

interventions.action: Administrar antiemético preventivo (p. ej., proclorperazina) según orden médica 30 min antes
interventions.rationale: Bloquea receptores dopaminérgicos en el CTZ

interventions.action: Crear ambiente tranquilo: luz tenue, minimizar olores fuertes
Reforzar educación sobre uso de técnicas de afrontamiento y registro de síntomas

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos
related_to: ansiedad que aumenta pérdida de fluidos
outcomes: Balance hídrico mantenido: I/O equilibrado en ±100 mL/24 h
Electrolitos (Na+, K+) dentro de rangos normales

Ofrecer líquidos claros en pequeños sorbos cada 15 min si la náusea está controlada

en.summary: Nausea that appears before starting a treatment, typically chemotherapy, as a learned response to the stimulus associated with the procedure.
key_points: Triggered by a conditioned association between the treatment environment and prior vomiting experiences.
Risk factors include anxiety, previous nausea experiences, female sex, and age <50 years.
Primary management is non-pharmacologic: relaxation techniques, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and systematic desensitization.
Antiemetics can be used prophylactically but are less effective than behavioral interventions.
Potential complications: dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and reduced treatment adherence.

pathophysiology: The environmental stimulus (chemotherapy room, odors) is associated with the CTZ via classical conditioning.
The brain anticipates nausea and activates the trigger zone of the chemoreceptor, releasing dopamine and serotonin.
A physiological nausea response occurs before exposure to the chemotherapeutic agent.
risk_factors: Previous nausea or vomiting during treatments.
Anxiety or fear of the procedure.
Female sex and age under 50 years.
Sensitivity to odors or visual stimuli in the treatment environment.
signs_symptoms: Subjective complaint of nausea before starting therapy.
Increased respiratory rate and abdominal discomfort.
diagnostics: Focused medical history of prior episodes and triggers.
Vital sign assessment and hydration status.
Laboratory tests only if dehydration suspected: Na+, K+ in mEq/L, glucose in mg/dL.
treatment: Deep relaxation and diaphragmatic breathing techniques before treatment.
First-line antiemetics such as phenothiazines (e.g., prochlorperazine) or 5‑HT3 antagonists (ondansetron) as a preventive measure.
Environmental control: reduce strong odors, dim lighting, and minimal noise.
complications: Interruption or delay of the chemotherapy regimen.
nursing_care: Assess nausea level using a 0‑10 scale before and after treatment.
Monitor intake and output; record I/O every 8 h.
Provide a calm environment, minimize triggering stimuli.
Administer antiemetic per prescription 30‑60 min before the procedure.
patient_teaching: Teach breathing and relaxation techniques to use before the session.
Inform about the importance of taking the preventive antiemetic as directed.
Identify and avoid stimuli that trigger nausea (odor, food).
Encourage adequate hydration and light meals before treatment.

outcomes: Controlled nausea: patient reports ≤2 episodes per day

interventions.action: Assess nausea level with a numeric scale before treatment
interventions.rationale: Allows quantification of intensity and monitoring of response

interventions.action: Apply diaphragmatic breathing and guided relaxation 10 min before the procedure
interventions.rationale: Reduces the anxiety response that triggers nausea

interventions.action: Administer preventive antiemetic (e.g., prochlorperazine) per medical order 30 min before
interventions.rationale: Blocks dopaminergic receptors in the CTZ

interventions.action: Create a calm environment: dim light, minimize strong odors
Reinforce education on coping techniques and symptom logging

related_to: increased fluid loss due to anxiety
outcomes: Maintained fluid balance: I/O within ±100 mL/24 h

interventions.action: Monitor intake and output every 8 h and record values
Offer clear fluids in small sips every 15 min if nausea is controlled
interventions.rationale: Prevents dehydration without overloading the stomach

interventions.action: Assess signs of dehydration (turgor, mucous membranes, blood pressure)
Administer antiemetic as indicated to reduce vomiting episodes
Educate patient on the importance of hydration and recognizing fluid deficit symptoms

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: Nausea and vomiting may occur as anticipatory, beginning before a treatment begins, or during or soon after a treatment.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Risk factors for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting include female sex, clients who experienced nausea and vomiting during pregnancy, age less than 50 years, and incidence of nausea and vomiting with previous chemotherapy treatments.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Risk factors for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting include female sex, clients who experienced nausea and vomiting during pregnancy, age less than 50 years, and incidence of nausea and vomiting with previous chemotherapy treatments.

sections.complications.1.quote: These include myelosuppression, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and electrolyte imbalances including hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia.

sections.complications.2.quote: Bone marrow suppression may be severe, requiring interruption of therapy.
